hero.intro: I'm **Victor Ajibodu**. I lead design at a **CBN-licensed fintech**, building products for real constraints: mobile-first, low-bandwidth, low-trust, high-stakes. Then I ship the numbers that show it worked.

manifesto.text: Most products don't fail in Figma. They fail in the gap between the brief and the real world: at the KYC wall, the broken checkout, the page nobody owns. That gap is where I work. I find the problem nobody wrote down, build the case with evidence, and ship the better thing.

projects.title: Fast Credit *Mobile App.*
projects.hook: How a branch-only lender reached 10,000 mobile users, by letting trust come before paperwork.
projects.summary: Nigeria's first unified finance app: savings, loans, investments and transfers in one CBN-licensed product. I led design end-to-end: 250+ alpha sessions, a progressive-KYC model that overturned the original PRD, a 60+ component design system, and a launch that onboarded 10,000 users.

meta.label: Scope
meta.value: Research · UX · UI · Design system · A/B testing

glance.problem: A regulated lender with branches but no digital product, and a KYC wall that lost users before they saw a single loan offer.
glance.solution: Progressive 3-tier KYC: earn trust first, ask for documents once the value is clear. After launch, a BVN-first flow that removed name-mismatch lockouts.
glance.impact: 10,000 users at launch, 80% onboarded on the first attempt, and roughly 70% fewer failed account upgrades.

items.label: Onboarding completion lift vs. the original PRD

blocks.heading: Branches, loyal customers, and *zero digital presence.*
blocks.body:
Customers drove to physical offices to apply for loans, check balances and start investments. Competitors were shipping apps. The company needed to move, fast.

The brief said *build a mobile banking app*. The harder question nobody had written down: **how do you onboard Nigerian users into a CBN-regulated product without losing them before their first loan?**

blocks.heading: 250+ alpha sessions before a single screen reached engineering.
blocks.body: I tested with the people Fast Credit actually serves: first-time app users, salary earners, market traders and civil servants. One friction point surfaced almost immediately: **the KYC wall.**

blocks.text: I don't want to give my BVN to an app I don't trust yet. What if something goes wrong? Can I call someone?
blocks.attribution: Civil servant, 34, Lagos · first-time fintech user

blocks.heading: The insight: users weren't refusing to share. *They were refusing to share everything, first.*
blocks.body: The original flow demanded full KYC (BVN, NIN, proof of address, employment details) before a user could touch any feature. Drop-off in testing was severe. Nobody objected to verification itself; they objected to handing over everything before the app had earned a moment of trust.

blocks.heading: When the research said the brief was wrong, I *called the meeting.*
blocks.body: The PRD specified a single-gate KYC flow, the standard for regulated products. My research said it would kill onboarding. I brought the PM, Head of Engineering and senior stakeholders into one room with drop-off data, real user quotes and an alternative that stayed fully inside CBN rules.
blocks.label: The proposal: progressive 3-tier KYC
blocks.text:
**Tier 1 · Phone number only.** Explore the app and see potential loan limits. Trust is built before documents are requested.

**Tier 2 · BVN + basic details.** Unlocks transfers up to ₦50,000/day and basic savings. Clear value before going deeper.

**Tier 3 · Full KYC.** Unlocks full loan access, higher limits and investments. By now the user has experienced the product and trusts it.

blocks.body: The team restructured the PRD around the tiered model and engineering rebuilt the verification pipeline. **It shipped**, and became the backbone of onboarding.

blocks.heading: Every edge case designed *before* the visuals.
blocks.body: Low- to high-fidelity flows mapped onboarding from splash to dashboard, including the messy states: number already registered, terms not accepted, slow networks, BVN validation in progress.
blocks.caption: Onboarding, OTP and dashboard-entry flows

blocks.heading: Built for trust and speed, *at the same time.*
blocks.body: Fellix for its rounded confidence. Brand green as the single primary action colour, carrying the Fast Credit identity through every touchpoint. A 390 × 844 baseline tuned for one-handed use on the mid-range Android phones most customers carry.

blocks.heading: Four modules. *One unified product.*
blocks.body: Home, Investments, Loans and a More panel with account upgrade, each built for real Nigerian conditions: patchy connectivity, older devices, and people making real financial decisions.

blocks.heading: Four screens, eight variants, *measured decisions.*
blocks.body: During alpha, four screens showed friction. I tested two variants of each and let the evidence decide before launch.
blocks.caption: A/B tests: Dashboard, Transaction history, Transfer and Loan

items.label: Dashboard
items.body:
**A:** minimal white layout with icon-only actions.
**B:** green hero card, Withdraw/Fund surfaced, recent transactions, SME-loan banner. Users oriented faster and explored more features in their first session.

items.label: Transaction history
items.body:
**A:** a date-grouped list.
**B:** search by bank or account, filter tabs and a calendar filter. A passive log became an active lookup tool.

items.label: Transfer
items.body:
**A:** two large icon buttons, an extra tap with no context.
**B:** a top toggle, recent-beneficiary avatars, source account, daily limit and a remark field. Less friction before commitment.

items.label: Loans: the biggest shift
items.body:
**A:** a red, centred *Apply now* with no repayment context.
**B:** outstanding balance up top, the active loan broken down (tenor, progress, monthly repayment), and Top-up for existing borrowers. Red became brand green. **A prompt became a financial-management tool.**

blocks.heading: 10,000 users in the first weeks. *80% onboarded on the first attempt.*
blocks.body: The 20% who didn't finish first time were mostly blocked by a BVN mismatch between their registered details and the national database, a data-quality issue outside the product. **Naming that distinction kept the team from "fixing" an onboarding flow that wasn't broken.**

blocks.heading: Then real usage exposed a failure *the tiers couldn't fix.*
blocks.body: Once people hit the BVN upgrade at volume, a quieter problem surfaced, one that's invisible in a demo. The flow asked users to **type their name alongside their BVN, then matched the two.** A real slice of Nigerians can't pass that match through no fault of their own: women who married and haven't updated their BVN, people whose BVN carries a legal name they never use, small differences in spelling or word order. The system read each one as a mismatch and silently blocked the upgrade.

blocks.text: My BVN still has my maiden name. The app keeps telling me my details don't match, but they are mine.
blocks.attribution: Recurring theme across post-launch support tickets

blocks.heading: The fix: *don't make users prove what the BVN already knows.*
blocks.body: Instead of typing details to be matched against a record, the user provides the BVN, proves they own it, and confirms what comes back. The name is never typed, so it can never mismatch.

items.title: Enter BVN
items.body: One field. Nothing to mistype.

items.title: Verify ownership
items.body: A one-time code goes to the phone number tied to that BVN.

items.title: Confirm details
items.body: We show the name and data pulled from the BVN; the user confirms it's them.

items.title: Liveness check
items.body: A quick selfie confirms a real person matches the verified BVN.

items.title: Secure the account
items.body: Set PIN and password. Upgrade complete.

blocks.label: Why the inversion works
blocks.text: The old flow made users responsible for a record they don't control. The new flow makes the **BVN the source of truth** and the user the **confirmer**, not the data-entry clerk. It also turns a dry compliance step into a trust moment: people see exactly which data is being used, and agree to it.

blocks.heading: One group the BVN-first flow *still can't fully reach.*
blocks.body:
Pull-and-confirm leans on one assumption: that the user can still receive a code on the number tied to their BVN. Some can't: numbers registered years ago by an enrolment agent, SIMs swapped or lost. We monitor and fund this, holding OTP friction at a managed **~7–8%**. But that is still real people, and it lands on the same group progressive KYC was built to protect.

The next move isn't another screen. It's a research-backed proposal to make verification lean less on a number the user can't control, without loosening a single CBN requirement. That work is underway: quantifying the failure, mapping who it hits, and testing an easier path to a verified account.

blocks.heading: What this project *taught me.*

items.label: Compliance ≠ friction
items.body: Regulation defines *what* you verify, not *when* you ask. Sequencing is a design decision.

items.label: Name the real failure
items.body: Separating product failures from data failures kept the team focused on problems we could actually fix.

items.label: Production tells the truth
items.body: The quietest failures only show up at volume. Support tickets are research, too.

projects.title: Fast Credit *Website.*
projects.hook: Nobody asked for this redesign. One overheard conversation, one evening's audit, and a calculator nobody requested.
projects.summary: Marketing said the site wasn't converting. Sales said leads arrived confused. Nobody owned the fix, so I did: an independent audit, six structural failures, a case to leadership, and a full redesign, including a loan calculator that became the most-engaged element on the site.

meta.label: Scope
meta.value: Audit · IA · UX · UI · Stakeholder case

glance.problem: A website that confused visitors and under-delivered for marketing and sales, with no one assigned to fix it.
glance.solution: A self-initiated audit, a consolidated information architecture, and a custom loan calculator that answers the visitor's real question: can I afford this?
glance.impact: 70% more engagement, lower bounce, and leads who arrived already understanding what they were applying for.

blocks.heading: I walked past a conversation. *That evening, I had the audit.*
blocks.body:
Marketing was frustrated the website wasn't converting. Sales said leads were arriving confused about what Fast Credit actually offered. Everyone felt the problem; nobody had a plan.

I ran an independent audit that evening. The picture was clear within the hour: **the site wasn't just dated; it had structural problems no amount of visual polish could fix.** The next week, I was in front of leadership with findings and a proposal.

blocks.heading: Six failures. *None could be solved by repainting.*
blocks.caption: Before: five sparse product pages, no hierarchy, weak calls to action

items.label: 01 · Dated
items.body: **No trust signals.** The visual design lagged the brand, costing credibility before a word was read.

items.label: 02 · Navigation
items.body: **A maze of five product pages** (Loans, Investments, Fast Thrift, Public Workers, BNPL) to understand one offering.

items.label: 03 · Overload
items.body: **Every page explained everything.** No hierarchy, no obvious next step anywhere in the journey.

items.label: 04 · Sparse
items.body: **Content spread thin.** Pages that needed depth were empty; pages that belonged together were siloed.

items.label: 05 · Imagery
items.body: **Generic stock photography** with no link to the brand or its customers, undermining trust instead of building it.

items.label: 06 · Layout
items.body: **No consistent grid.** Arbitrary spacing and broken rhythm made the site feel assembled in parts.

blocks.heading: Five sparse pages became *one purposeful structure.*
blocks.body: The first decision was structural, not visual: consolidate navigation so every product earned its place in the hierarchy. Then I added something no stakeholder had asked for but every visitor needed: **a loan calculator**, answering the only question that matters before applying: *can I afford this?*
blocks.caption: Desktop and mobile wireframes: restructured IA and the new loan calculator

blocks.heading: A homepage that finally *tells the story.*
blocks.body: A clear value proposition. Trust signals up front: CBN-licensed, Bbb-rated by Augusto & Co. App downloads surfaced, products consolidated, benefits explained, testimonials and partners as proof. The whole pitch reads in one scroll.
blocks.caption: Shipped homepage: hero, products, benefits, testimonials, partners

blocks.heading: Every page rebuilt, including *the one nobody asked for.*
blocks.body: About, every loan product, the calculator, blog, and contact with office locations, designed at desktop and mobile breakpoints.
blocks.caption: About, Loans, Fast Pearl, Calculator, Blog, Contact

blocks.heading: 70% more engagement. The unrequested calculator became *the most-used thing on the site.*
blocks.body:
Engagement rose 70% and bounce rate fell. Sales reported a shift in lead quality: customers now arrived already understanding what they were applying for.

The calculator was never in a brief, because nobody thought to put it there. **That's the work I value most: the thing that wasn't assigned, but needed to exist.**

blocks.heading: What this project *taught me.*

items.label: Initiative needs evidence
items.body: An audit turned a hallway complaint into a mandate. Opinions start debates; evidence starts projects.

items.label: Design for the decision
items.body: Visitors weren't asking for more pages. They were asking *can I afford this?* The calculator answered it.

items.label: Structure before style
items.body: Consolidating the IA did more for clarity than any visual change could have.

projects.title: Evamor *Store.*
projects.hook: A premium water brand was losing orders to its own website. Rebuilt around one job: ordering from any screen.
projects.summary: Evamor sells premium alkaline dispenser water to homes, offices, hotels and restaurants across Lagos. The product was excellent; the website was the bottleneck. I rebuilt it around a single job: getting an order placed from any screen. Conversions rose 35% in three months.

glance.problem: Visitors couldn't find how to order, the mobile experience broke, and the order form asked too much, too early.
glance.solution: A sitemap rebuilt around purchase intent, a persistent Order Now path one click from anywhere, and a one-page order form with transparent pricing.
glance.impact: 35% more conversions within three months, driven mostly by mobile, and 20% sales growth in the first year.

items.label: Click to order, from any page

blocks.heading: A strong product. *A website working against it.*
blocks.body: Evamor Water is a premium Nigerian brand: alkaline, BPA-free, 5-gallon dispenser bottles for health-conscious homes, offices, hotels and restaurants across Lagos. The product was excellent. The website was the bottleneck, and it was costing sales at every step.

items.label: 01 · Navigation
items.body: **Order Now was hidden.** You had to already know it existed. The IA assumed familiarity the visitor didn't have.

items.label: 02 · Mobile
items.body: **Most Nigerian traffic is mobile**, and the site buckled there: awkward layouts, mistuned touch targets, inconsistent type.

items.label: 03 · Checkout
items.body: **The order form asked too much, too early,** with no context on delivery or price. People abandoned before submitting.

blocks.heading: The path to purchase: *one click from anywhere.*
blocks.body: I rebuilt the sitemap around the visitor's real intent (understand the product, trust the brand, place an order) and made Order Now persistent on every page.
blocks.caption: Wireframes: Home, About, Products and Order · desktop and mobile

blocks.heading: Deep ocean blues. *Trust, by association.*
blocks.body: A palette of ocean blues to signal purity, quality and trust. Poppins for clean neutrality that stays legible on small, bright screens.

blocks.heading: Home, story, products, order: *one cohesive flow.*
blocks.body: About (mission, vision, values), detailed product pages with specs and benefits, and an order page rebuilt for clarity: name, address, phone, a quantity selector and transparent pricing, all on one screen.
blocks.caption: Home, About, Core values, Products and Order

blocks.heading: From digital brochure to *acquisition channel.*
blocks.body: Three months after launch, conversions were up 35%, with the biggest gains on **mobile**, the segment the old site had failed. By the end of year one, sales had grown 20%, and the website was working as a genuine acquisition channel rather than a digital brochure.

blocks.heading: What this project *taught me.*

items.label: IA is conversion design
items.body: The biggest lift came from moving one path to the surface, not from a new coat of paint.

items.label: Design for the real device
items.body: Mobile drove the gains. Designing for the phone in your customer's hand isn't optional in Lagos.

projects.title: Cedaa *Yoghurt.*
projects.hook: Twenty years of craft, hidden behind a template. Three weeks to make the website as good as the yoghurt.
projects.summary: A Nigerian dairy with 20+ years of heritage, NAFDAC and SON certification, and a loyal customer base, all represented by a generic template with no mobile design. In three weeks I delivered a refined identity, a 12-column design system, and a mobile-responsive site that finally reflects the brand.

glance.problem: A premium product line undermined by a template site: no identity, no brand story, no mobile experience.
glance.solution: Evolution, not revolution: keep the brand's equity, refine it into a deliberate system, and give every product room to sell itself.
glance.impact: A mobile-ready brand platform in three weeks, with a system the team can extend without breaking it.

blocks.heading: Every ingredient of a premium brand. *A template undermining all of it.*
blocks.body: Cedaa had 20+ years of operation, NAFDAC and SON certifications, a loyal customer base across Ogun State, and a product line that deserved shelf space next to national players. The website was the one thing working against them.
blocks.caption: Before: a generic template: flat identity, no emotional pull, no mobile layout

items.label: 01 · Identity
items.body: **No brand presence.** A generic pink hero and slider; nothing signalled quality, heritage or a 20-year story.

items.label: 02 · Mobile
items.body: **No mobile design.** FMCG buyers research on their phones, especially for home delivery. Desktop-only meant invisible.

items.label: 03 · Products
items.body: **Good photography, buried** in a flat grid with no hierarchy, no variants and no reason to choose.

items.label: 04 · Story
items.body: **Factual but cold.** Mission, vision and values were listed, never felt.

blocks.heading: Evolution, not revolution. *Elevate the brand, don't replace it.*
blocks.body: The brief was elevation, not a rebrand. I kept the existing red and white and refined them into a deliberate palette, with a warm off-white base that lets product photography breathe. Urbanist brings confident geometry, premium without feeling cold.

blocks.heading: A site Cedaa's team can *scale on their own.*
blocks.body: A benefit-led hero (*Deliciously nutritious. Made for every moment.*), a catalogue tabbed by flavour (Vanilla, Unsweetened, Strawberry, Pineapple), Our Story, Why Cedaa, Core Values, a store finder with maps, newsletter and a full footer. Responsive throughout.
blocks.caption: Hero, Products, Story, Why Cedaa, Values, Find a store, Contact

blocks.heading: From template to *premium brand platform*, in three weeks.

items.label: Brand elevation
items.body: A premium identity that communicates quality, heritage and trust, without starting from scratch.

items.label: Scalable system
items.body: 12-column grid, documented components and tokens. New pages and campaigns ship without breaking the design.

items.label: Mobile-first
items.body: Full mobile alongside desktop, so customers can discover, explore and locate Cedaa on any device.

items.label: Product storytelling
items.body: Each flavour gets its own space: sizes, taste notes, nutrition callouts and photography that makes it desirable.

blocks.heading: What this project *taught me.*

items.label: Elevation is restraint
items.body: Keep the equity people already recognise; remove the noise around it.

items.label: Systems outlive launches
items.body: Three weeks of work only compounds if the team can extend it without me.

process.title: From idea to live, *in three acts.*
process.intro: Not a rigid template, but the through-line behind every project here. Find the real problem, build the system that answers it, then ship and prove it moved.

steps.label: Act I · Understand
steps.title: Find the *real* problem, not the one in the brief.
steps.body: Interviews, alpha sessions, analytics, competitor teardowns. On Fast Credit I ran 250+ sessions before a screen reached engineering, and the research overturned the original PRD.

steps.label: Act II · Design the system
steps.title: Design every edge case, then *build the system.*
steps.body: Every messy state resolved before the visuals, then tokens, components and documentation so the team ships consistently and fast. Progressive KYC was born here.

steps.label: Act III · Ship & prove
steps.title: Test, ship, then *measure what moved.*
steps.body: A/B tests where friction showed, a clean handoff, and honest post-launch numbers. Design isn't done when it's pretty. It's done when the metric moves.

services.title: What I bring to *your team.*
services.intro: Product design isn't pixels. It's making the right thing exist, with the research, rigour and stakeholder alignment to move a business outcome.

items.title: Product design
items.body: End-to-end design across mobile, web and SaaS, from problem definition to production-ready specs.

items.title: Design systems
items.body: Component libraries, tokens and documentation that cut handoff time and keep design and engineering aligned at scale.

items.title: Research & strategy
items.body: Research that surfaces the problem behind the brief, and testing that validates real decisions, even when the data points away from the plan.

items.title: Product partnership
items.body: I don't stop at delivering files. I find the problem behind the brief and build the case for the better answer.

about.pageTitle: I design products that *work in the real world.*
about.pageLead: Not just in Figma. Not just in pitches. **In production, with real users, in real conditions.**
about.body:
I'm Victor Ajibodu, a Lead Product Designer in Lagos with 6+ years building digital products across fintech, e-commerce and SaaS. I currently lead design at **Fast Credit Limited**, the CBN-licensed fintech behind Nigeria's first unified finance app.

I work where **user research, systems thinking and product strategy** meet. Most of my work serves Nigeria and the wider continent: mobile-first, low-bandwidth, high-stakes contexts where the user can't afford a bad experience and the designer can't afford assumptions. The constraints make the work sharper.

I don't wait to be asked. **The Fast Credit website redesign was self-initiated.** The progressive KYC that became the backbone of onboarding came from overturning the original brief with research. The loan calculator was never in scope, until I put it there.

The work I'm proudest of is rarely the work that was assigned. It's the gap nobody had words for, the problem everyone felt but nobody had named. **That's where product design earns its keep.**

Lagos isn't a constraint. It's the proof of competence.
